name: Chloe Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a haul truck at a large mine, hauling ore down to the crusher on early shifts. I'm 58 and still one of the junior hands; I can drive the route, but I ask when a machine sounds wrong instead of acting clever. I like that the day has a shape. The dust gets into the seals and into your socks, and the hydraulic leak on my assigned truck keeps coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the pit I'd say the fancy software has found its proper size: a quicker form, not a new driver. My shift still starts before sunrise and ends with a wash bucket full of grey water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our truck is older than some of the supervisors, and breakdowns worry me more than AI talk. My partner Len's warehouse hours have been uneven, so even a dull year doesn't feel secure at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my assigned truck shifts and ask maintenance about its recurring hydraulic leak. In the first year of that slow change, I'd put a little from each full pay packet into the car-payment account rather than buy anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, not frightened by the software. The thin part of the month is when both our hours wobble, and that was true yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill makes the uneven hours visible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car payment is the one I circle on the kitchen calendar. We have about four months of expenses saved, but I don't want a repair bill to eat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Len after a normal shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Len the mine looks much the same, and ask whether his warehouse rota has settled. The uncertainty in our house comes from ordinary pay packets too.

say: I'd tell the crew **routine software** won't replace the person steering the truck this year.
Our **pay packets** still depend on shifts and working equipment.
think: I worry more about **breakdowns** than a program while I operate the truck.
My partner's **uneven hours** mean the household is not truly settled.
do: Keep operating my **assigned truck** and report its hydraulic leak to maintenance.
Set aside money from each **full pay packet** for the car payment.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary hours and repairs, with little new fear from AI.
S0.quote: The uncertainty in our house comes from ordinary pay packets too.
fieldNote: Chloe watches the **car payment** because both household incomes can vary, even in the mildest scenario.
She talks plainly about the **truck leak** and places current mine maintenance ahead of distant technology.

steps.text: Keep taking assigned haul-truck shifts and report the hydraulic leak
Set aside money from full pay packets for the car payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say scheduling software may make the supervisors quicker, but a screen doesn't clear loose rock from my route. I would ask whether the mine plans to fill openings when drivers leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paperwork is small; the seat and the road are the job. Still, if office vacancies disappear and robots follow, management may decide an older junior driver is the easiest person to leave out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about haul-crew vacancies at the next briefing and keep my assigned shifts while they exist. During the first year, Len and I would cut the weekend trips to our grown daughter's place if either set of hours falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a cut that arrives a person at a time, without one dramatic announcement. I'm too close to needing steady earnings to treat it as interesting news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the next shift briefing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift supervisor whether vacancies in the haul crew will actually be filled. I would not pretend I can learn a whole new machine from a notice pinned up at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the change touches Len?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Len's warehouse job uses rosters and order records, and those could shrink earlier than mine. We need to look at his hours before we call our household safe.

say: I'd ask whether **haul vacancies** will be filled as software takes planning and booking work.
Our crew still handles **loose rock** and awkward routes that a screen can't clear.
think: My **driving work** lasts longer than office tasks, but a smaller crew is plausible.
My partner's **warehouse hours** may be cut by changes in records and scheduling.
do: Ask my supervisor about **haul vacancies** at the next briefing.
Keep taking **haul shifts** while the mine still assigns them.
Cut **weekend travel** to our grown daughter's home if either income falls.
feel: **Anxious** about slower losses of hours across both earners.
S1.quote: I'm too close to needing steady earnings to treat it as interesting news.
fieldNote: She separates **driving** from scheduling, while admitting a smaller operation may reduce crew openings.
The prospect of lost **warehouse hours** makes this scenario a household concern before mine robots arrive.

steps.text: Ask the shift supervisor whether haul-crew vacancies will be filled
Cut weekend trips to the grown daughter if household hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is no proper warning for the people who run the pit. Full thinking AI in 2028 may take the office work first, but I would want the mine to tell drivers what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 60 in 2028 and 63 when capable robots reach the trucks around 2031. I cannot assume a pension starts just when a machine can take my seat, and four months' savings is no bridge to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep hauling in 2028, and ask management for its written staffing timetable before the robots reach our work. In that first year I'd record each week's hours and stop booking our annual seaside holiday until Len and I see our income clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes me alarmed, even though I have a short stretch in the truck after the first AI arrives. I can see a finish line for this job without seeing the start of retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the first year after 2028, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be hauling ore because the robots in this picture arrive around 2031. I'd ask for the mine's written staffing timetable and keep records of my hours so I can see any slide early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Len before our grown children; they're building their own lives, not a fund for us. I'd say we need to stop the annual holiday booking until we know what the mine intends.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028 AI** reaches mine planning before it reaches my truck.
Our managers owe drivers a **staffing timetable** before robots arrive around 2031.
think: I would be **60 in 2028** and still need wages.
Four months of **savings** won't carry me from robot arrival in 2031 to an unknown retirement date.
do: Keep **hauling ore** through 2028 while hands-on robots are still three years away.
Ask management for a **written staffing timetable** and record weekly hours.
Stop booking the **annual holiday** until our income is clearer.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely loss of driving income before any known retirement income begins.
S2.quote: I cannot assume a pension starts just when a machine can take my seat, and four months' savings is no bridge to retirement.
fieldNote: At **60 in 2028**, she expects to keep driving but wants warning before robots can do it around 2031.
She refuses to count on **pension timing** she has not established or support from grown children.

steps.text: Keep hauling ore during the first year after 2028 AGI
Ask management for the written robot staffing timetable and record hours
Stop booking the annual seaside holiday until income is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the crew a chance to ask hard questions, not a promise that the mine will keep us. At 63 in 2031 I might still be driving while the office has full AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2034 put me at 66, close to when I hope to leave, but hope isn't an income plan. I need to know what our actual retirement money and household costs look like before I say we're safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and ask payroll for the retirement statements I have never put in one folder. In the first year after 2031, I'd check the statements with Len, ask the mine for its vehicle-transition timetable, and take funded training on new vehicles only if it is offered in a patient way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried but less cornered than in the two-year picture. Time helps me count properly; it doesn't make the robot date disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do with five years that you cannot do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Len and I could sit down with our statements each winter and work out the gap after wages stop. I could also ask the mine what training it would fund on the newer vehicles, though I would need someone to show me slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does asking about training mean you want a new career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it means I want to keep earning as long as the mine has a seat for me. Starting a wholly new trade at 63 feels like a hard bet with our savings.

say: I'd tell the crew **2031 AI** may change planning while drivers remain at work until robots around 2034.
Five years gives us time to demand **clear dates**, not a guarantee of work.
think: At **66 in 2034**, I may still need the truck wage.
My retirement hope needs **actual figures** before I can rely on it.
do: Keep **driving** during the first year after 2031 AGI.
Check **retirement statements** with Len and ask the mine for vehicle-transition dates.
Take **funded vehicle training** if the mine offers patient instruction.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check retirement figures before robots can take driving work.
S3.quote: Time helps me count properly; it doesn't make the robot date disappear.
fieldNote: She treats five years as time to gather **retirement statements**, rather than assuming a pension will cover the gap.
Her willingness to train is **conditional** on funding and patient instruction, fitting her reluctance toward new technology.

steps.text: Keep driving mine trucks in the first year after 2031 AGI
Check retirement statements with Len and request mine transition dates
Take funded vehicle training if the mine offers patient instruction

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time for the mine to give ordinary drivers a straight answer about robots. At 68 in 2036, I'd hope to be home more, but some people my age still need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm still on the roster at 68, thinking AI could strip away the office tasks in 2036 while I continue driving. Robots reach hands-on work around 2039, when I'd be 71; I must plan for stopping before then without pretending I know the pension figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the truck while the job is there and gather our debt and retirement statements now. In the first year after 2036, if I am still on the roster, I'd review those figures with Len and apply for suitable nearby equipment shifts if our income needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than trapped, provided our figures show a path out. I still dislike the thought of a robot taking the work before I have chosen to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you start now if that were the timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd gather our retirement and debt statements this winter and decide with Len what monthly income we'd need. I would keep the truck job rather than gamble on another trade, then review whether we can afford to leave when the numbers are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the numbers say you cannot leave at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask for another shift or a suitable nearby equipment job while I can still do the physical work. Some similar mines are within reach, but I would not call a vacancy guaranteed.

say: I'd say **ten years** gives drivers a fair chance to plan for the 2039 robot date.
I might still need **paid shifts** at 68, so retirement cannot be assumed.
think: I want to stop before **robots in 2039** if our money allows it.
My actual **retirement income** is still an unknown figure, not a promise.
do: Keep taking **truck shifts** while the mine assigns them.
Gather **debt and retirement statements** and review affordability with Len after 2036.
Apply for **nearby equipment shifts** if household income still needs wages in 2037.
feel: **Uneasy** about the retirement gap, though a decade allows a measured plan.
S4.quote: If I'm still on the roster at 68, thinking AI could strip away the office tasks in 2036 while I continue driving.
fieldNote: At **68 in 2036**, Chloe may still need paid work and does not declare herself retired.
She would consider **nearby equipment applications** in 2037 if the household figures show wages remain necessary.

steps.text: Keep taking mine truck shifts while assigned
Gather debt and retirement statements and review them with Len
Apply for nearby equipment shifts in 2037 if wages remain necessary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be 60 when the thinking work changes and only 63 when the robots can drive. Four months' savings won't cover an unknown stretch between my last wage and retirement income. A written mine timetable and a real check of our retirement statements would help me make choices instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the people who drive older equipment get shown the new controls properly, one person at a time. I learn slowly, but I can learn when somebody lets me practice instead of handing me a screen and walking away.

headlineQuote: I can see a finish line for this job without seeing the start of retirement income.
portrait: Chloe is a **58-year-old junior** haul-truck operator at a large mine who still asks for help with unfamiliar equipment.
Her partner Len's **uneven warehouse hours** and their car payment make today's income uncertain despite four months' savings.
She fears **2031 robots** could end driving wages before she knows when retirement income begins.
With more warning, she checks **retirement figures** and keeps paid work available instead of assuming she can stop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because robots arrive around 2031, before she knows how retirement income will bridge lost wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written mine timetable** and checked retirement statements would help Chloe plan before driving work changes.
She wants **patient vehicle instruction** if the mine offers training on unfamiliar controls.
